**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — As tensions within Iran over the disputed presidential election continue to escalate, President Obama should reach out to Iranian opposition leader Mir Hossein Moussavi, a former Bush administration official told CNN on Sunday.

Paul Wolfowitz, who served as deputy defense secretary during the Bush administration, shared his perspective with CNN's Wolf Blitzer. "I would certainly find out if he [Moussavi] wants a conversation," Wolfowitz said. "If he doesn't, I certainly wouldn't push it. But I would make it clear that the phone line remains open."

On Saturday, Obama released a written statement addressing the bloodshed in the streets of Tehran, where demonstrators have gathered to protest the election results. "The Iranian government must understand that the world is watching," the statement read. "We mourn each and every innocent life that is lost.

"We call on the Iranian government to cease all violent and unjust actions against its own people. The universal rights to assembly and free speech must be respected, and the United States stands with all who seek to exercise those rights."

Nevertheless, Obama has drawn criticism from some lawmakers and analysts who argue that he should articulate a more resolute position on the unfolding clashes.

*Watch the latest videos being leaked out of Iran »*

"I understand the concern about meddling in a way that seems to label the opposition as American tools, but the opposition has made it very clear that they want support from the world," said Wolfowitz, a staunch advocate of the U.S.-led war in Iraq and a scholar at the American Enterprise Institute.

CNN Senior Political Analyst David Gergen echoed this sentiment, adding, "It would be useful for the president to demonstrate more forceful leadership on the international stage regarding this issue." Citing the graphic images emerging from Iran—including the fatal shooting of a young female protester identified as Neda—he observed that the violence calls for "some kind of humanity from the West."

Both Gergen and Wolfowitz maintained that the United States should unite with other Western nations, and even with countries in the region—including Afghanistan and Turkey, both of which have recognized incumbent President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad as the winner of the June 12 election—to stand in support of the Iranian people.

Ahmadinejad's victory was declared by Iran's election authority, the Guardian Council, a decision that sparked massive protests last week, with many demonstrators voicing their support for Moussavi. Moussavi, along with candidate Mehdi Karrubi, has denounced the election as fraudulent and called for a new one.

Wolfowitz described Moussavi as a "very brave man," noting, "He is resisting. He is putting his life at risk."

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- As the standoff in Iran over the contested presidential vote grows more intense, a onetime Bush administration figure suggested Sunday that President Obama ought to establish contact with Iranian opposition figure Mir Hossein Moussavi.

Paul Wolfowitz, who served as deputy defense secretary under President Bush, shared his views with CNN's Wolf Blitzer. "I would certainly find out if he (Moussavi) wants a conversation," Wolfowitz remarked. "If he doesn't, I certainly wouldn't push it. But I would make it clear that the phone is an open line."

A day earlier, on Saturday, Obama released a written statement addressing the violence unfolding on Tehran's streets, where protesters were challenging the election results. "The Iranian government must understand that the world is watching. We mourn each and every innocent life that is lost," the statement read. It continued, "We call on the Iranian government to stop all violent and unjust actions against its own people. The universal rights to assembly and free speech must be respected, and the United States stands with all who seek to exercise those rights."

Despite this, various politicians and commentators have faulted Obama, arguing that he ought to take a firmer public position regarding the confrontations.

Wolfowitz, a prominent advocate of the American-led conflict in Iraq and a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, acknowledged the risks but pushed back. "I understand the concern about meddling in a way that seems to label the opposition as American tools, but the opposition made it very clear they want support from the world," he explained.

Echoing this view, David Gergen, CNN's Senior Political Analyst, stated that "it would be useful for the president to show more forceful leadership internationally on this issue." Pointing to the disturbing footage coming out of Iran -- among them the deadly shooting of a young woman protester known as Neda -- Gergen argued that such bloodshed demands "some kind of humanity from the West."

Both Gergen and Wolfowitz maintained that Washington should join forces with fellow Western nations, as well as regional players such as Afghanistan and Turkey -- both of which have acknowledged sitting President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad as the victor of the June 12 vote -- in backing the Iranian population.

The Guardian Council, Iran's election oversight body, had proclaimed Ahmadinejad the winner, triggering enormous demonstrations the previous week, during which countless protesters declared their allegiance to Moussavi. Both Moussavi and fellow contender Mehdi Karrubi have dismissed the vote as rigged and called for it to be held again.

Wolfowitz described Moussavi as a "very brave man," adding, "He is resisting. He is putting his life at risk."

In the wake of Iran's contested presidential election, mounting evidence of fraud, and increasingly brutal government crackdowns on demonstrators, prominent voices from across the political spectrum called on President Barack Obama to adopt a more assertive posture toward the unfolding crisis. Among those urging a firmer response were former Deputy Defense Secretary Paul Wolfowitz and veteran political analyst David Gergen, both of whom argued that the administration's measured approach was inadequate to the moment.

The disputed election, in which incumbent President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the winner over opposition candidate Mir Hossein Moussavi, had ignited widespread protests throughout Iran. As demonstrators poured into the streets to challenge what they viewed as a stolen election, Iranian security forces responded with escalating violence. Graphic images and videos depicting bloodied protesters and fatal confrontations began circulating widely, drawing international attention and horror.

Wolfowitz and Gergen contended that the United States should raise its voice more forcefully in response to these developments. They suggested that President Obama consider reaching out directly to Moussavi, signaling American support for the opposition movement and the Iranian people's aspirations for a fair electoral process. Such a gesture, they argued, would demonstrate clear moral leadership at a critical juncture.

Their recommendations echoed a broader chorus of criticism emerging from lawmakers and foreign policy analysts. Many of these critics maintained that Obama's initial responses—delivered primarily through carefully worded written statements—failed to match the gravity of the violence unfolding on the ground. The President had adopted a deliberately cautious tone, seemingly wary of allowing the Iranian regime to portray the protests as a product of American interference.

However, as the death toll rose and the images of suffering grew more disturbing, pressure intensified for the administration to abandon its restraint. The debate reflected a deeper tension over the role the United States should play on the international stage, and whether principled rhetoric or strategic caution best served American interests and values during a moment of profound uncertainty in Iran.

**Washington (CNN)** — Paul Wolfowitz, a former deputy defense secretary under President George W. Bush and a key architect of the Iraq War, is calling on President Barack Obama to take a stronger stance in support of Iran's opposition movement amid mass protests over the country's disputed presidential election.

In an opinion piece and public comments, Wolfowitz argued that the United States should more openly voice support for Iranians challenging the official results that declared incumbent President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad the winner over opposition leader Mir Hossein Moussavi.

Wolfowitz invoked the legacy of President Ronald Reagan, suggesting that Obama could follow the example of a president who spoke out on behalf of dissidents behind the Iron Curtain during the Cold War.

"When Ronald Reagan condemned martial law in Poland, he was criticized for interfering in Poland's internal affairs," Wolfowitz wrote, drawing a parallel to the current situation. He argued that moral clarity from American leaders can matter to those risking their lives in the streets.

## A Debate Over Obama's Approach

The comments add to a growing chorus of criticism, particularly from Republicans and conservatives, who argue that the Obama administration's measured response has been too cautious.

Obama has said he does not want the United States to become a scapegoat that Iran's ruling clerics could use to discredit the opposition as agents of foreign interference.

"It's not productive, given the history of U.S.-Iranian relations, to be seen as meddling," Obama said, defending his approach while condemning the crackdown on demonstrators.

## Critics on Both Sides

Other prominent Republicans, including Sen. John McCain and Sen. Lindsey Graham, have echoed calls for the president to speak more forcefully in defense of Iranian protesters.

Supporters of the administration's strategy counter that overt American involvement could backfire, playing directly into the hands of hardliners in Tehran who have long characterized opposition movements as tools of Western powers.

The debate reflects a broader tension in U.S. foreign policy over how America should respond to popular uprisings against authoritarian governments — balancing moral support for democratic aspirations against the risk of undermining the very movements it seeks to help.

# International Response to Violence Against Protesters Following Iran's 2009 Election

## Background

The June 2009 Iranian presidential election triggered one of the most significant waves of civil unrest in the Islamic Republic's history. When incumbent President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the winner with a substantial majority, supporters of opposition candidate Mir-Hossein Mousavi took to the streets in protest, alleging widespread electoral fraud. The demonstrations that followed became known as the "Green Movement," named for the campaign color adopted by Mousavi's supporters.

The government's response to these protests was forceful. Security forces and the Basij militia confronted demonstrators, resulting in numerous injuries, deaths, and mass arrests. The death of Neda Agha-Soltan, a young woman shot during a protest whose final moments were captured on video and shared globally, became a powerful symbol of the crackdown and galvanized international attention.

## The Obama Administration's Measured Approach

The administration of President Barack Obama, then only months into its first term, faced a complex diplomatic challenge. Obama had entered office signaling a willingness to engage diplomatically with Iran over its nuclear program, representing a departure from the confrontational posture of his predecessor.

In the early days of the unrest, the administration adopted a deliberately restrained tone. Obama expressed concern over the violence while avoiding language that could be interpreted as direct interference in Iranian internal affairs. His initial statements emphasized that the outcome should be determined by the Iranian people, and he expressed reluctance to have the United States appear to be "meddling."

This calculated caution reflected several strategic considerations:

- **Historical baggage:** The 1953 U.S.-backed coup that overthrew Iran's democratically elected Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh remained a potent memory. American officials feared that vocal support for protesters could allow the Iranian regime to portray the movement as a foreign-orchestrated plot.

- **Diplomatic goals:** The administration hoped to preserve the possibility of negotiations with Tehran on nuclear issues, and worried that harsh rhetoric might foreclose that avenue.

- **Effectiveness concerns:** Some officials questioned whether strong American statements would actually help protesters or merely provide the regime with propaganda ammunition.

## Domestic Criticism and the Push for Stronger Action

The administration's restraint drew significant criticism, particularly from Republican lawmakers and commentators who argued that the United States had a moral obligation to support those risking their lives for democratic principles.

Prominent critics, including Senator John McCain and Senator Lindsey Graham, contended that America's silence effectively abandoned the protesters. They argued that the United States should unambiguously stand on the side of those seeking freedom, regardless of diplomatic calculations. To these critics, the moment represented a test of American values and leadership.

The debate crystallized a fundamental tension in American foreign policy: the competition between **realist** approaches, which prioritize national interests and pragmatic engagement, and more **idealist** or values-driven approaches, which emphasize the promotion of human rights and democracy.

As the violence continued and images of the crackdown spread, the Obama administration gradually sharpened its language. Obama eventually stated that he was "appalled and outraged" by the violence and threats against protesters, marking a notable shift from his earlier caution.

## The European and International Reaction

European nations often adopted more forceful positions than Washington. France and Germany, among others, issued sharp condemnations of the violence. The relationship between Iran and several European governments deteriorated as diplomatic tensions escalated, including disputes over the treatment of foreign nationals and embassy staff.

Various international bodies and human rights organizations documented abuses and called for accountability. However, meaningful action through multilateral institutions was constrained by geopolitical realities, including the positions of countries reluctant to condemn Tehran.

## The Limits of Intervention

The debate over the appropriate response ultimately underscored the limited options available to outside powers confronting internal repression in a sovereign state. Direct intervention was never seriously contemplated, and the practical tools available—diplomatic statements, symbolic gestures, and potential sanctions—offered no guarantee of influencing events on the ground.

Some analysts argued that the most valuable contribution the international community could make was ensuring that communications channels remained open, allowing Iranians to share information and organize despite government efforts to restrict internet and mobile networks. The role of social media platforms in the protests drew particular attention, illustrating how technology was reshaping both protest movements and international awareness of them.

## Aftermath and Legacy

The Green Movement was ultimately suppressed, with opposition leaders placed under house arrest and the protests gradually subsiding under sustained pressure. The nuclear negotiations that the Obama administration had hoped to preserve would eventually culminate in the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, though the path there proved long and contentious.

The episode remains a significant case study in the enduring dilemmas of foreign policy. It raised questions that continue to resonate: How should democratic nations respond to the suppression of popular movements abroad? When does support become counterproductive interference? And how should governments balance strategic interests against moral commitments?

The 2009 Iranian protests and the international response they generated illustrated that these questions rarely yield clear answers, and that the choices facing policymakers in such moments involve profound uncertainty about both the ethics and the effectiveness of intervention.

## A Contested Outcome

Moussavi, a former prime minister who campaigned as a reformist alternative to incumbent President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, has refused to accept official results declaring Ahmadinejad the winner by a wide margin. His campaign alleges numerous irregularities in the vote counting process.

"I ask the people to continue their nationwide protests in a peaceful and legal way," Moussavi said in a statement to supporters, while calling for the results to be annulled.

The opposition candidate, who had drawn massive crowds during the campaign's final days, has become a symbol for many Iranians seeking greater social freedoms and improved relations with the West.

## Government Response

The Iranian government has defended the election as legitimate. The Guardian Council, the body responsible for certifying results, has said it would examine some complaints, though critics remain skeptical of any meaningful review.

Reports of clashes between demonstrators and security forces have emerged, along with restrictions on internet access, mobile communications, and foreign journalists' ability to cover the unrest.

## The American Debate

The disputed election has sparked debate in Washington over how President Barack Obama should respond.

Some analysts and lawmakers have urged the president to speak more forcefully in support of the demonstrators.

"The president should be standing up for the aspirations of the Iranian people," argued critics who contend that American silence risks appearing indifferent to democratic movements abroad.

Others caution that overt U.S. involvement could backfire, allowing Iranian hardliners to portray the opposition as agents of foreign interference.

"If we are seen as meddling in this election, it could undermine the very people we want to support," said foreign policy observers advocating a more measured approach.

The Obama administration has thus far struck a careful tone. The president expressed concern over the violence while emphasizing that the outcome should be determined by Iranians themselves.

"It is up to Iranians to make decisions about who Iran's leaders will be," Obama said, adding that he was "deeply troubled" by the images emerging from the country.

## What Comes Next

The situation remains fluid, with the scale and duration of the protests testing both the opposition movement and the government's response. Observers say the coming days could prove pivotal for Iran's political future and its relationship with the international community.

*This is a developing story.*
